title: The Multiplier Effect of Impact Capital
gist: A BCG survey of 114 foundations, family offices, HNWIs and advisors finds that the old philanthropic model—prove a solution, let government scale it—is breaking under fiscal pressure, pushing funders toward "impact-first" capital (recoverable grants, guarantees, first-loss and concessional debt) explicitly designed to pull in third-party commercial money. Awareness is high (~75%) but allocation is low (21%), with the top blockers being a shortage of investable deals, impact measurement, and—strikingly—advisors who find the instruments harder to understand than their own clients do.

insights.claim: The traditional philanthropic pathway—funders prove out evidence-backed solutions in education, health or climate and public-sector systems then scale them—is becoming unreliable as fiscal pressure and shifting policy priorities squeeze government budgets.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Capital that used to hand off to governments now has to find private co-investors instead, creating structural demand for blended-finance structuring, guarantees and concessional debt products.
insights.quote: Philanthropy has been based on proving out models that the government will scale. That overarching thesis is at risk.
insights.locator: Leaders of foundations and family offices

insights.claim: A relative decline in public-sector investment is expected to widen the gap between impact capital flows and the need, making mobilization of sideline private capital the defining constraint rather than the supply of good intentions.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Expect fee-earning opportunity for whoever can originate and standardize blended structures; the bottleneck is intermediation, not donor appetite.
insights.locator: Impact capital flows have always been scarcer

insights.claim: Funders are increasingly dissolving the historic wall between philanthropic pools and traditional investment portfolios, pursuing impact objectives across a combined pool spread along the full risk-return spectrum.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Asset managers should expect impact mandates to be assessed against the whole balance sheet, not a ring-fenced grant budget—widening the addressable pool well beyond the 5% payout slice.

insights.claim: US grants and donations reached a record $617.2 billion in 2025, with foundations accounting for 19% of the total, up from roughly 7% four decades ago, according to the Giving USA Foundation.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Institutional foundations now control a structurally larger share of giving than individuals did historically, concentrating decision-making into a smaller set of professionalized buyers of financial structures.
insights.locator: Grants and donations reached a record

insights.claim: Between $320 billion and $330 billion sits pre-committed but undeployed in donor-advised funds, according to the DAF Research Collaborative.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: A third of a trillion dollars of already-irrevocable charitable money is parked and addressable—any product that unlocks DAF deployment into recoverable structures targets an unusually captive pool.

insights.claim: Market-rate impact investing—debt and equity intended to produce social or environmental impact alongside commercial returns—runs at roughly $50 billion annually per the Global Impact Investing Network, while reliable figures for annual impact-first flows do not yet exist.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: The absence of flow data for the impact-first segment is itself the investable gap—data infrastructure and benchmarks are a prerequisite for scale, and an early-mover niche.

insights.claim: Nearly 75% of surveyed funders say they are familiar with impact-first capital instruments, but only 21% report a high allocation of assets to that category.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: The awareness-to-allocation gap is the entire commercial opportunity: distribution and structuring, not education about the concept, is what converts interest into flows.

insights.claim: The survey deliberately skews toward already-engaged participants—114 respondents of whom roughly 70% were US-based, about 60 foundations, 21 HNWI/private banking clients, 19 family offices and 14 advisors—and its authors read the results as a leading indicator from active players rather than the market as a whole.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Treat the reported enthusiasm as an upper bound; if even self-selected practitioners allocate only 21%, broad-market penetration is far thinner than headlines suggest.

insights.claim: BCG estimates more than half of total emissions could be abated with solutions that are already cost competitive, which is precisely why market-rate capital has flooded into solar, storage and EVs.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: The cheap half of decarbonization is already a crowded commercial trade; incremental returns there are competed away, pushing alpha into the uneconomic tail.

insights.claim: Roughly 45% of needed decarbonization sits below cost parity, and about one-third of that portion is at a meaningful—not marginal—cost disadvantage, leaving technologies that commercial investors will not touch first.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Roughly 15% of the abatement task needs deep subsidy or concessional structures to ever be bankable—useful for sizing where grants, first-loss tranches and guarantees, not equity, are the right instrument.

insights.claim: Restoring degraded cropland in Brazil's Cerrado to regenerative agriculture is expected to require about $31 billion of catalytic capital plus $6 billion of mostly philanthropic grants to unlock $24 billion of commercial capital, restoring 9 million hectares worth an estimated $55 billion in increased production.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: A concrete capital-stack template with a quantified multiplier—note the leverage runs below 1x on concessional dollars, a sober benchmark against marketing claims of 10x mobilization.

insights.claim: Adaptation and resilience splits sharply: some solutions such as engineered flood defense already attract return-seeking investors, while others generate real socioeconomic value without ever producing a bankable return.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Screen adaptation deals by whether a cash-flow-bearing asset exists at all; the non-bankable half will never clear a commercial hurdle no matter how urgent the need.
insights.locator: The same dynamic holds in adaptation

insights.claim: Enosis Capital's Debt-for-Nature Private Credit Enhancement Facility has already drawn family office capital into debt-for-nature swaps, a structure historically funded only by foundations and banks.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Evidence that private wealth follows once a structure is proven—watch sovereign debt-for-nature issuance as a leading indicator of private credit entering conservation finance.

insights.claim: Global health's defining market failure sits on the demand side: the people who most need new vaccines and drugs live in countries whose health systems cannot pay enough, or predictably enough, to attract commercial investment.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Explains why health blended finance instruments are narrow and demand-guaranteeing (AMCs, volume guarantees, price stabilization) rather than the capital-stack layering used in climate.

insights.claim: Blended health financing almost always mixes public and philanthropic money rather than private-sector sources, unlike climate deals where private commercial capital is the intended destination.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Tempering signal for anyone underwriting health impact funds: the private capital crowd-in thesis has far less empirical support in health than in energy or land use.

insights.claim: The 2009 Pneumococcal Advance Market Commitment pooled $1.5 billion from five governments and the Gates Foundation to guarantee demand for a vaccine low-income markets would not otherwise attract, and COVAX revived the same structure at scale during COVID-19.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Advance market commitments are the one health instrument with a repeated, scaled track record—the template to expect in future pandemic-preparedness and NCD financing.

insights.claim: MedAccess has codified the volume guarantee as an instrument, with a portfolio that has supported products reaching 559 million people across more than 115 countries.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: A proven guarantee platform at scale is exactly the 'mature structure with a track record' that lets balance-sheet capital underwrite health risk without bespoke diligence.

insights.claim: Gavi's latest replenishment raised just over $9 billion against an $11.9 billion ask, while the pledging summit unlocked $4.5 billion from development finance institutions, a €1 billion European Investment Bank liquidity facility, $4 billion pledged by implementing countries to their own immunization programs, and a $1.2 billion accelerator for African vaccine manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Donor shortfalls are now routinely backfilled by DFI leverage, liquidity facilities and domestic co-financing—a durable shift in who funds global health and which balance sheets carry the risk.

insights.claim: Noncommunicable diseases cause about three in four deaths worldwide yet draw under 2% of development assistance for health, and MedAccess is testing a pay-per-use radiotherapy guarantee in Kenya and Tanzania as a first foray into the category.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: The largest mortality burden is the least-funded category—an emerging demand pool for medical device and oncology equipment makers if pay-per-use guarantee structures work.

insights.claim: New health taxes in low- and middle-income countries are flagged as a potential future funding source for guarantee-backed private-sector health activity.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Watch sin-tax and health-levy legislation in LMICs as the fiscal precondition for domestically financed health procurement replacing donor money.

insights.claim: The most frequently cited barrier to deploying impact-first capital is a lack of sufficient investable opportunities, followed by the difficulty of measuring impact, the time required to evaluate deals, and missing internal capabilities.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Deal-origination infrastructure, not capital, is the binding constraint—platforms that source, structure and pool transactions capture the scarcity rent.

insights.claim: Smaller foundations and family offices lack in-house specialist teams to evaluate and execute impact-first deals, while larger ones typically have those capabilities, producing a two-tier market by asset size.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Capability-as-a-service—syndicated structuring teams or co-investment vehicles anchored by large foundations—is the obvious product gap for the long tail of smaller allocators.
insights.locator: A particular constraint cited in interviews

insights.claim: Funders interviewed often do not recognize that a deal they have already sourced could be structured or funded with a non-grant instrument, defaulting to grants even when a better-suited tool exists.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Latent demand is larger than stated demand; conversion depends on instrument literacy at the point of deal review, which is where advisors and banks can insert themselves.
insights.quote: Interest in impact investing is outpacing action; a lot of resources out there on this [ecosystem] do not correctly identify or address the barriers to greater participation.
insights.locator: In our interviews, meanwhile, funders acknowledge

insights.claim: Satellite imagery is being used to track forest and farm carbon storage, and AI analysis of large research data sets can surface previously unseen relationships between health interventions and outcomes, easing the measurement burden without loading work onto resource-constrained grantees.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: MRV and impact-verification tooling is a picks-and-shovels play on impact capital growth, since measurement is the number-two cited barrier.
insights.locator: At the same time, meaningful strides

themes.theme: The advisor gap and the wealth transfer

insights.claim: Some 42% of advisors call impact-first instruments too complex or hard to understand—more than twice the share of foundations (19%), family offices (13%) and high-net-worth individuals (6%)—meaning the intermediaries are more confused than their clients.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: The capital bottleneck sits in the distribution layer; wealth platforms that train advisors first can capture flows their competitors are actively deflecting.

insights.claim: HNWIs and family offices name finding the right advisor and legal structuring—not complexity of the instruments themselves—as their top obstacles to deploying impact-first capital.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Demand exists and is searching for supply of competent intermediation; legal and fund-formation specialists serving this niche have a clear addressable market.
insights.locator: HNWIs and family offices instead point

insights.claim: Cerulli Research indicates only 20% to 27% of heirs retain their parents' wealth advisor after an inheritance, making fluency in impact-first investing a retention hedge against the coming wealth transfer rather than an optional specialty.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Attrition math gives wealth platforms a hard commercial reason to build impact capability now; watch which private banks productize it as a differentiator ahead of the transfer.
insights.quote: For advisors, fluency in impact-first investing may no longer be a “nice to have” but instead a hedge against the coming wealth transfer.

insights.claim: Some leading universal banks have begun routing opportunities originated by their clean energy investment banking teams to private wealth clients, bridging institutional origination with individual balance sheets.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Cross-divisional origination is the emergent model—banks with both a clean energy franchise and a large private bank have a structural advantage in this market.
insights.locator: Some leading universal banks have started

insights.claim: The impact-first market is described as opaque and therefore slow, because investors cannot readily see how much catalytic or concessional capital is available, the terms required, or how comparable transactions were structured.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Price and terms discovery is the missing market utility; the G7's Catalytic Capital Repository is the venue to watch for whether transparency reaches critical mass.

insights.claim: Today's impact-first market consists largely of bespoke one-off transactions, and moving to guidelines, standards and common metrics would let participants compare, replicate and underwrite faster—with British International Investment, the Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero and BCG having built a framework for blended finance funds toward that end.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
entities: Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero
insights.so_what: Standardization is the precondition for securitization and secondary liquidity; adoption of these frameworks is the metric that signals the asset class is becoming investable at scale.
insights.quote: We need a catalytic library for structures, with mature structures that have a proven track record.

insights.claim: Foundations with deal-structuring capability are urged to offer syndicated expertise—effectively renting out their teams to family offices and HNWIs—turning internal capability into market infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Large foundations become de facto GPs for private wealth; HNWIs are already drawn to co-investing alongside them for diligence capacity, which is a distribution channel in disguise.
insights.quote: High-net-worth individuals are primarily drawn to co-investing with larger institutional foundations because they value their expertise and their capacity to perform due diligence.

insights.claim: Recoverable grants are recommended as the entry instrument for family offices because downside is capped at the grant amount and any repayment is pure upside, enabling a staged progression from grant to recoverable grant to concessional loan.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: A concrete on-ramp product: whoever standardizes recoverable-grant documentation captures the first rung of a ladder that ends in much larger concessional debt allocations.
insights.quote: What resonates with the board is showing that impact investing offers a sustainable pathway to impact, and seeing money come back from program-related investments (PRIs).

insights.claim: Wealth managers are advised to move from bespoke deals to repeatable playbooks that codify structuring and diligence so impact capital transactions become standard offerings rather than one-offs for a single client.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Productization converts a cost center into a margin and retention driver; it is also the mechanism by which volumes scale enough to matter to capital markets.

insights.claim: Governments are positioned less as funders of last resort than as enablers—supplying highly concessional funds that combine with private dollars, building public-sector capability to partner with the ecosystem, and setting regulation such as rules around philanthropic giving.
insights.speaker: Naomi Desai
insights.so_what: Regulatory change around philanthropic giving and DAF/PRI rules is the policy lever most likely to move hundreds of billions in parked capital—a specific legislative watch item.

top_entities: Glasgow Financial Alliance for Net Zero
